I regret pouring almost 900 hours into a game that began to die mere months of my first time playing, on December 23rd, 2012. This day was just 3 days after the last update that added weapons for more than 1.5
The only content they added between the
and The
was purely cosmetic. All cosmetics also began to decrease in value. Around this time, the economy went right down the toilet. There were a lot reasons for such a massive crash, including corruption (backpack.tf), inflation (idlers), and an artificial decrease in price (quicksellers). People desperately tried to sell off their inventories. Needless to say, a lot of people lost a lot of money. To give an example, Earbuds, a rare promotional item from the launch of Team Fortress 2 on the [garbage] OS X platform, were valued at USD $53.50 in 2013, their point of equilibrium. In late 2015, their price was estimated at just over $6. When their supply was estimated in January 2016, and it was found that it was lower than projected, their price stayed stable, showing the inherent lack of demand in trading the game has today. You may be thinking "Oh it's just an item, who cares." Well, Earbuds were a
They experienced inflation not seen since the Deutschmark in Germany after WWI. Keys, the next major currency, were once worth 2-3 refined metal (yet another currency) were hyperinflated during 2014, skyrocketing to 11 refined and above. Now as of the date of this review, Mann Co. Supply Crate Keys sit at the horrifying price of 20 refined metal. Assuming there are no special drops, it would take 18
to grind for a virtual item worth a mere $2.50. So basically, don't try to trade in Team Fortress 2, it will never end well.
In terms of actual gameplay, it took the clowns

years?

Where would I need to start on this game? Honestly there are mixed opinions on this game and writing this review in 2016 after 4 years of staying away from this game and avidly playing it I can come to one conclusion. If I am going to play /one/ FPS game forver in my life it will be TF2.
1. Restricted headshots: I'm honestly really really bad at aiming, I can at least aim in the 'general' direction but headshots? Seriously those are a big no for me (not getting any better after years) and thankfully in TF2 only a handful of weapons can do that so I don't have to worry about them too much.
2. Classes: Yes some classes are countered by certain classes so hard it's enough to rage quit but it's just how the game flows. If there's something bad because of that then it's rather to play games like CS:GO that has no such form of classes
3. Customizing: No not customizing how your character looks, how the character takes on different weapons and how to use them. One man's garbage can become another's treasure. Trying out some stupid loadouts can spart the fun time to time.
4. Nothing is unimportant: Each class has problems when stacked, but none of the class at all can become a serious problem. It really encourages teamplay even in 16:16 matches and I am really happy about that. Even if it's a newbie that just learned how to fire a gun it still helps in some way possible.
5. Silly moments: Sometimes, a certain situation is so random that I can't help but to laugh with it.
6. Easy to start, but unlimited skill cap: When you get better, there is always someone who is better that you in something. Placement, intuition, aiming, luck, awareness. and etc. Everthing has some room to get better and better as you try out the game.
7. Free: A big, no huge advantage over anything. Just try out the game, understand the mechanics and go forward. If you don't like it you can safely drop it. No problem at all.
8.
I'll add onto the list I can think of in the future, but definately. If I only could play one FPS in my life it would be TF2. Yes I date to say even over Overwatch which in June 19, 2016 is a marching giant over anything.

*Downloads Tf2

Honest Review:
Honestly, Tf2 is a great free to play first person shooter with so many different weapons and fun classes to play as. Personally, I really think that the game is a lot more fun and unique compared to other F2P models out there. Unlike most other games, it's not PayToWin which means that you don't have to pay actual money to get better at the game and instead of that you require to spend time to actually become better.
Some of the things that I dind't enjoy could be hackers, even though you rarely ever see them they still can ruin the game, most of the time they spam the exact same message in chat and it takes quite a while for them to actually get kicked or banned. I also found that the community could be quite toxic sometimes but that's not the main concern, because of the latest 'Find Your Match' update it is a bit hard to find an actual good server because Valve removed their Pub Servers which makes it a little bit hard, I mean I could go on community servers but you know how bad they are (considering that most of them are trade servers).
Tf2 trading is another topic i want to talk about, the game is rich with many in-game items such as hats, weapons and much more, they can be traded which is why trade servers exist and hundreds of trades are made each day. Because of that you can easily make some money if you want to buy a specific game or a steam item, using myself as an example, I've gotten nearly every single game in my library for free just by trading Tf2 items, it is a fun thing to do if you enjoy trading and getting other things. Anyway, a small problem with that are scammers, it is quite rare to encounter one but they still exist, those type of people will try to get all your items using several methods of scamming.
However I really enjoyed Team Fortress 2 and in my opinion it deserves an 8/10 rating from me.

*** LONG REVIEW ***
I've reviewed this game twice before, so I decided to just make a brand new one that will last for even when I don't play. Going on 1600+ hours and beyond, TF2 has stolen my heart and will not let go. I had played 1400 hours and decided to take a break because I was bored with the game and thought that Overwatch would kill it. With that thought in my mind, I decided to give Overwatch a try. I had only played Overwatch for about 20 hours and got bored. It's repetitive, the community is toxic, the whole nine. I'll be honest, I feel as if I wasted $40 on Overwatch, but that's my mistake. After this happened, I decided to reconnect with the friends I had made through TF2 that I had basically abandoned. And even though I abandoned them, they did not abandon me. They welcomed me back with open arms, and I even met some new people that had hopped into the Discord we had started long ago. Ever since, my love of TF2 has returned, and even with college fast approaching (tomorrow as of writing this), I hope that I will still have to time to play this game. Whatever your tastes are, and whatever you have heard about this game being dead, give it a try. I promise that as of writing this, TF2 is not even close to dying. It will continue to hold it's own as new class-based shooters come out. I know this was a long review, but I greatly enjoy this game and hope that millions more will continue to long after this. The time will come when Valve will fully abandon this game, but I will keep playing until then.

Well I took down my last review ranting about the updates and instead I'll give my experience with the game.
TF2, well, I guess I'll start from the begining of my experience.
2010/2011/2012 or something like that, I started my experience with this game with my small computer. I can still remember the excitement I felt every time I loaded up a game with casual, community severs and the like, it felt great to dish out bullets and dodge rocket wizzing right towards you while your team fights rulthlessly against the other for the objective.
The hats and weapons were down right insane with the amount of customization you could match up with them. You could demolish someone with a space bazooka or turn a frighteningly giant man with a machine gun into a snack weilding buddy who's soul purpose is to toss sandwiches.
My personal favorite class would have been the spy since you could easily get up close and personal with the enemy. With the spy, you could sneak right up to the enemy lines unseen and impersonate one of the team members while destroying sentries and other high value targets. I loved the idea of this but I wasn't quite the master of stealth and got blown up 95% of the time.
Now as a side topic, around 2011-2013, there was this sort of prejudice against F2Ps and how they weren't fit for the game and how they were just noobs that deserve to be shamed. Now I'm not going to ride a high horse and pretend I didn't do this myself because, as a matter of fact, I took some part in this but came to the relization that it was wrong but if you see a F2P, show them some love and give them some ways to aid them in gameplay.
Well, I was having a blast with this whimsical game right up until October 2013. It was this change and I could feel it. Something was off and not right about the game. Maybe it was the file size when I went to reinstall it or maybe it was the lack of content with no new bosses. I don't know for sure but I felt that magical sensation of the game disapait from then on.
Now I just really can't install it because, well, I think I've just moved on. Maybe I might revisit it in say a couple of weeks/months/year, but I'm not to sure on it because everytime I come back for that sweet sensation I have experienced so many years ago, it just gets worse for me.
Well I guess this goodby until we meet again in the future old friend.
Thank you for the memories Valve and have a happy rest of 2018 (I know I'm kinda late to the party but still)

Tf2 is the gateway to PC gaming for a lot of people and it was the same case for me, it introduced me to steam, and how it functions. Not only did Tf2 introduce me to steam, it's a great game, and through the many years I have played the game, it has remained one of my favorites.

I will tell you a story of Team Fortress 2's golden age.
The game used to have a variety of weapons to pick from, flourishing community servers, a playerbase that ranged from tolerable to friendly, and hours of well-deserved play time.
The only time this game ever crashed was when you ran it on a potato. It also had full support for Directx 9, which I used when Team Fortress 2 began to lose frames due to updates. It used to be around 8-10 gb upon my first install.
The TF2 trading community wasn't always a fun aspect, but I can say I definately came out of it in the green. Without TF2 items, I may have had to pay for Civilization 5 by spending more than two keys for it. I would save up my 8 refined metal and trade it off to other players for keys.
I can't say I was a huge fan of Halloween Updates. Merasmus and the Horseless Headless Horseman weren't really fun games to play in. Monoculus, however, was one I actually enjoyable.
All good things must come to an end.
Weapons nerfs have created a situation where all the items in the game are (usually) worse than stock. At this point in the game, what is the point in getting new items? The new items were intended to be a different way to play the game, but players always succeed by using what they already have.
Matchmaking today only put the nail in the coffin of community servers. Community servers mostly died off by the introduction of the previous matchmaking algorithm in place. They added a button to add them into the search: a small little button. This was abused by servers, such as Saigns, which had modified versions of the game, which led TF2 to take down that feature. Well-intentioned servers, such as Firepowered and Skial, took the punishment as well.
Maybe I'm just older, and less tolerant to the annoying things people do nowadays. To me, though, TF2's community went from tolerable and friendly to cancerous and intolerable. It was hard for me to play with them.
With new updates, Team Fortress 2 requires more CPU and GPU power than ever before. Longtime players of this game have dealt with performance issues almost never dealt with before, and that is disheartening. To make matters worse, using Directx 9 makes the game very tough to work with, sending you out of their new competitive matchmaking system, which isn't even something I wanted from them in the first place. Sad.
This Hat Simulator actually has too many hats. People wanted hats, but they should've been more careful for what they wished for. It's hard to say that this is the reason it takes 15gbs today, but it certainly is a factor. The newest gamemodes they added were very much extra and not what most players were looking for in a first person shooter.
I learned that the TF2 developers hired an economist to look at the TF2 economy, since the refined metal count continues to grow while the key value remains constant. Now a key costs 27.44 refined metal, and the economist who worked on the TF2 community has moved on to look at the Greek economy. From this point, I invite any reader to look at the greek economy today.
The Halloween update with Merasmus and the Go-karts seemed to be the best one yet. I was excited for that Halloween update. Once I got done with playing it, I deleted my achievement melee weapon I hated it so much. It was the least amount of fun I have ever had playing a Team Fortress game, period. The go-karts were a complete bust, the gamemode was horrible, and the reuse of Merasmus was everything I wasn't hoping for. They could have done SO much better, but, what can we do?
At one time, I would have been happily playing this game any time I wanted, but from here on, I would want to see major changes before I consider joining back into the fray.
I invite you all to play it if you wish, but if you ever get frustrated with anything they add, well, know that you aren't alone.

One of the most fun games I've ever played, and that's saying a lot.
I haven't had that long of an experience in TF2 than most players had, but I remember downloading Steam in 2014 just to test out this amazing game that everyone was recommending me to play. And so, even though I haven't been playing since 2010 or even 2013, there were many things in the two years I've played this game that made it memorable and made it feel like playing 40 hours a week of just one game is worth it.
1. The content. Now that competitive matchmaking in-game is coming up, Valve hasn't put much effort into anything else. Just some crap balances for SOME weapons (cough Phlog cough) and skins (new maps as well, but screw them). However, now that Overwatch is out, Valve will certainly start becoming more aware of their players and losing players to Overwatch. Which is good. And, to make things even better, there's already a 9-year history of infamous bugs, insane community mods, awesome weapons, and random crits.
2. The high skill cap. Because TF2 is such a highly skill-based game, there's no end to it. I, personally, love games that don't focus on a campaign, and have alternative playstyles, just like Minecraft, a game I played a few years ago before I got into Team Fortress 2. There's just so much that there is to the game, and so many different ways to take. For example, rocket jumping alone may take years to master, and trickshotting as sniper isn't as easy as you'd think it is. Having only 750 hours in the game when this review is posted, there's still much for me to learn.
3. TF2. Muselk has a few videos entitled "Just TF2 Things", which is listing the unique parts of Team Defense Fort 2. For example, there are almost always going to be Gibus noobs and random crits, which are just a few things that make TF2 unique. The cartoony, violent style of your surroundings is an example. Hats. And of course, Scout's voice. I want an accent like that.
4. The "replayability" of the game. As mentioned in number 2, there's many things you can explore, many paths you can take. Finding the best sentry spot to hold last in Badwater for 10 minutes? Possible, but may take a long time. Learning how to double sticky jump? May also take a long time. Avoiding spies? Impossible.
5. Did I already say hats?
That's going to be it, this is the most I've typed in a long time. I'm going to play TF2 now.

They added a button to add them into the search: a small little button. This was abused by servers, such as Saigns, which had modified versions of the game, which led TF2 to take down that feature. Well-intentioned servers, such as Firepowered and Skial, took the punishment as well.
Maybe I'm just older, and less tolerant to the annoying things people do nowadays. To me, though, TF2's community went from tolerable and friendly to cancerous and intolerable. It was hard for me to play with them.
With new updates, Team Fortress 2 requires more CPU and GPU power than ever before. Longtime players of this game have dealt with performance issues almost never dealt with before, and that is disheartening. To make matters worse, using Directx 9 makes the game very tough to work with, sending you out of their new competitive matchmaking system, which isn't even something I wanted from them in the first place. Sad.
This Hat Simulator actually has too many hats. People wanted hats, but they should've been more careful for what they wished for. It's hard to say that this is the reason it takes 15gbs today, but it certainly is a factor. The newest gamemodes they added were very much extra and not what most players were looking for in a first person shooter.
I learned that the TF2 developers hired an economist to look at the TF2 economy, since the refined metal count continues to grow while the key value remains constant. Now a key costs 27.44 refined metal, and the economist who worked on the TF2 community has moved on to look at the Greek economy. From this point, I invite any reader to look at the greek economy today.
The Halloween update with Merasmus and the Go-karts seemed to be the best one yet. I was excited for that Halloween update. Once I got done with playing it, I deleted my achievement melee weapon I hated it so much. It was the least amount of fun I have ever had playing a Team Fortress game, period. The go-karts were a complete bust, the gamemode was horrible, and the reuse of Merasmus was everything I wasn't hoping for. They could have done SO much better, but, what can we do?
At one time, I would have been happily playing this game any time I wanted, but from here on, I would want to see major changes before I consider joining back into the fray.
I invite you all to play it if you wish, but if you ever get frustrated with anything they add, well, know that you aren't alone.

This is my first review, and it is really late, so no guarantees about the quality of this one. Also, I'm not sure I'm qualified given I only have a few hundred hours on TF2.
TF2 really is a great game. I'd have to say one of the things I like best about TF2 is the personality it seems to have. It never takes anything too seriously, and you can always join a server and expect to have fun, regardless of whether you are winning or losing, fighting or not fighting. It is centered around fun and is a great game to play if you are looking for a laid-back escape from the dire straits of everyday life. Everything from the graphics to the sounds to the taunts even to the outlandish mechanics is geared towards entertainment. And this personality is not specific to the feel of the game; the players are focused on making the game an enjoyable experience for everyone, not just themselves or their own team.
For example, right now I just spent over an hour right after midnight playing with the only other person on a certain server, and I mean playing, not fighting. He taught me some tricks and even died a few times so I could perform certain glitches. We just hung out, despite being on opposite teams, and had a great time. Most people I meet are amiable like this, and that changes the whole game so that it feels like you are always playing with friends.
Now, what did I dislike about the game? Well, I'm not sure there's any singular, glaring annoyance that makes TF2 not a great game. Sure, there's some notable ones like random crits, phlog pyros, gunslingers, and autobalance, but even these have a reason and many would make the game less fun if they were removed, despite the irritation they have potential for.
All together, TF2 is simply a great game, and I hope everyone reading this will want to play it with me.
Sincerely,

TF2 deserves a real review from me because I just have to much to say about it. Out of all the games I've played in my entire life, I must say that
is one of THE best so far. It hasn't failed yet in keeping me crawling back to it to play each day, and each time I do play it I have a blast. Most people will instantly enjoy the game upon picking it up and it will keep you hooked for a good 150+ hours. I have to say that it's probably the most addictive drug I've ever taken (and I haven't taken any drugs lmao).
Gameplay is one of the main factors of what makes this game so damn great. There is a total of nine different classes to chose from, each with their own set of skills and arsenals. Certain classes counter other classes, and so on and so forth. The game mechanics are, or used to be, very balanced with the exceptions of a few classes and weapons. The game is relatively stable with only some bugs that Valve usually fixes. Emphasis on usually. Just hop on a server, pick your class, and kick some♥♥♥♥♥ That being said, it's a great game to have some kooky fun in with friends, or alone, if you're like me.
Graphically, the engine TF2 was created on shows its outdatedness. Textures look pretty cheezy, the phong shading looks only halfway decent, reloading animations pretty bad on certain weapons, and models look like they were made from two and a half polygons because Valve can't be bothered to count to the third polygon. However, when cranked to Ultra High, the game can pretty okay looking for a Source game.
Despite this being a very old game the community is still very active. This feeds features such as an ingame economy and animated shorts created by the devs. You can trade with players for things like cosmetics, weapon skins, and weapons with the ability to count your kills with said weapon. You need not spend more than $5 to unlock trading abilities for your account but once you do you can trade up to cosmetics with special particle effects worth up to $16,000 ♥♥♥♥ing dollars. How cool is that? Virtual pixels worth $16,000!
The community for this game is what you'd expect from most online communities, e.g. toxic competitive players, 12 year old F2P scrubs, memelords, and content creators like YouTubers. The competitive scene is pretty decent, with leagues like UGC and ESEA and semi-competitive sites like TF2Center. TF2's built-in matchmaking system is currently in utter dismay and I heavily recommend not wasting your time with it, but this is subject to change. The creative scene for this game is incredible and you're probably not going to find such dedicated creators elsewhere. Tons of YouTubers, streamers, animators, mappers, and artists are 'round the clock making interesting and exciting content for your viewing experience.
Alas, what goes up must come down. TF2 will start to disappoint once you start wanting more, fresh content that Vavle seems to be unable to deliver. Because of this, you will eventually burn yourself out on this game. For me, it happened around 1,500hrs of playtime but I know that it has held off until approximately 4,000hrs for my other friends. The economy in its current state is in a depression, with the main form of currency being extremely inflated. Escrow discourages lots of traders from even attempting to trade. The game is rather unoptimized as it's such an old game which was made on such an old engine, ping makes a very large difference in the game, and bugs take Valve three weeks to fix once they even acknowledge that they exist. Hackers run rampant in matchmaking as Valve hardly does anything to smite them. Despite this, you will never be able to rid yourself of the addiction that TF2 puts you through.
- Great community, it's pretty hard to find the bad parts of it
- Lots of community created content
- Good competitive scene
- Loads of cosmetics and character customization
- Loads of weapons
- Nine different classes with interesting game mechanics to back them up
- Lots of maps to explore and play on
- Lots of game mechanics to explore
- Decent graphics & netcode
- Highly addictive
- It's free
- Hackers
- Bad matchmaking system
- Most game mechanics need a lot of rebalancing
- Rarely updated
- Becoming neglected by Valve
- A few gamebreaking bugs here and there
- Unoptimized for newer machines / throttles the CPU and hardly touches the GPU
- Community servers are pretty bad
- Ingame economy is in a horrible state
I rate this game in its current state at
for being good with some pretty critical issues, like the stale content, hackers shutting down your entire 6s team, certain weapons and classes being extremely overpowered and underpowered, and just the general neglect that Valve has put it through.

Team Fortress 2 (TF2) is one the games that you really have to try, it is Free to Play (F2P) and has an outstanding unique first-person shooter (FPS) style. Unlike most FPS that is played competitively, it focuses more on fun and especially humor. TF2 has a various types of character classes and game modes, a bunch of maps and hats (yes you read it right, HATS!).
TF2 is fun yet a challenging game, it has a rich gameplay and a huge community. It is composed of two opposing factions represented by the name of these companies, the Reliable Excavation & Demolition (RED) and Builders League United (BLU) which are mercenaries hired by two opposing brothers. Players can choose any classes, characters and the side they represent to compete against the opposing team through certain missions/objectives per game mode.
Unlike most FPS games, TF2 has a lot of good game modes, every game mode has a different and unique play style which makes the game interesting. Other game modes are still in beta stage thus small bugs might occur but overall  it has a decent maps, objectives and team play. Here's a list of game modes and its respective mission/objective:
The best map for beginners would be King of the Hill, its simple yet fun.
Most FPS games focuses more on weapons and less on characters, in TF2 you can get to choose 9 different characters with unique roles and special abilities. The game is created to have fun thus expect a unique approach on certain abilities. Here's a list of classes and characters with their respective roles and characteristics:
Classes, Characters and team can be changed while the game is in progress. This can be done by pressing ", (comma)" to change class and character and by pressing ". (period)" to change team.
Just like most FPS games, TF2 uses the standard keyboard set-up which is the basic WASD (forward, move left, backward and move right) movement, R to reload, Q for last weapon used and etc. Mouse is used to aim (point), shoot (left-click), use every character's special skill (right-click) and to change weapon (mouse wheel up or down). The controls are smooth and comfortable, weapons can be changed through the keyboard with keys: 1, 2 and 3/4, 5 and 6 or through the mouse button by scrolling up or down.
The game is good to have fun and to kill some time but with more FPS games coming around its hard to keep up. I recommend this game for non competitive ones and for those who just want to play a good F2P FPS game, it has smooth and comfortable controls with decent character model and animation. Overall, this game is unique and better than any other FPS games, it has a strong game play and outstanding maps but if you are into a more competitive side, this game is simply not for you but absolutely worth the try.

Okay, this is coming from the perspective of a guy who has no home internet, so my hours are well over 200 (Small, but drones are boring, I'll get to that), versus the like, 2 hours that Steam says I have.
Darn internet.
Anyhow, look. Most of the reviews here will complain about a crude and monsterous cycle that has you join multiplayer, die instantly, rage, etc. I'm here to show you a different perspective.
Prepare..
-The Cycle of a Mainly-Offline TF2 Player-
-Join TF2
-Hey look, stuff to b- oh wait no internet.
-But.. the shop has a picture of a hat..
-Must... Have... Duck...
-Spend the next five hours trying to hack your neighbor's wifi signal.
-Fail.
-Dangit.
-Decide to actually try the game on this "Practice" mode.
-Join match full of drones.
-Laugh as you say "HAHA THE ENGINEER GUY IS SLAMMING HIS FACE INTO HIS WRENCH THING HAHAHA"
-Realize that you spent an entire minute laughing
-Run out, get butchered by sentry
-Rage and say..
-You guys guessed it..
-FIre..! PYROOOOOOOO
-Call a medic over, have him stalk you, dominate as pyro, get a 35 killstreak
-Win match
-Try a different mode
-Try KOTH
-Ooh, I can spam as Pyro too!
-End up perfecting your Pyro techniques after multiple matches lasting a total of 100 hours
-"You know, I think I'm pretty good at this! Library wifi, here I come!"
-Go to the library, use wifi to join a multiplayer match
-Pick Pyro, ofc
-Spend literally the entire match in your base screaming "MEDIC!!!"
-Get no kills
-Attempt again, with no medic
-Get 4 kills in total by randomly burning invisible spies, gotta love just using that flamethrower on literally everything
-Get called a noob Pyro that spams and has no friends, along with various racial slurs of course
-Bust out crying
-Decide, "Hey, if Pyro is a noob class, why not try something else?"
-Pick Soldier
-Rinse and repeat.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding cheese cake recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1 cup digestive plain sweet biscuit crumbs
3 tablespoons sugar
3 tablespoons melted butter
40 ounces softened cream cheese
1 cup sugar
3 tablespoons flour
1 tablespoon vanilla
1 cup sour cream
4 eggs
Directions:
For The base:.
If you're using a dark pan, preheat the oven to 350. If you are using a shiny pan, 375.
Combine the crumbs, melted butter and 3 tbsp sugar well and pat onto the bottom of a 9 inch springform pan. I also like to very very lightly butter the sides of the pan so that the cheesecake will not stick later on.
Bake for 10 mins in your preheated oven and remove. Let it cool while you prepare your batter.
For the batter:.
Make sure everything is at room temperature.
Combine sugar, cheese, flour and vanilla in a big bowl and mix on medium speed till well combined. Don't forget to scrape the bowl as you're doing this.
Mix in the sour cream till its incorporated well. Then, add the eggs one by one, mixing well after each addition.
Pour the batter into the springform and let it bake for 1 hour and 10 minutes After the baking time, turn off the oven and leave the door ajar. Let the cake cool in there for about 1 1/2 hours.
Remove the cake and let it cool thoroughly. Refrigerate overnight.
Release the sides of the springform.
Eat.

TEST OF TIME AWARD!!!
I'm going to say this outright.
Team Fortress 2 is one of the, if not the single best shooter games out there. There\'s just so much that makes it unique and interesting to keep you on your toes, discovering all new things every time you play. There\'s so much content in it and enough crazy antics and fun gameplay to keep you going for hours. I currently have 57 hours on record and I\'m gaining more and more just because of the sheer amazingness of it.
Pros:
The gameplay is one of the best things about TF2. The controls are easy to use, but also modifyable to your needs. There\'s tons of diverse game modes like capture the flag and such to choose from. You have the choice from nine extremely distinct and equally interesting classes (Scout, Soldier, Pyro, Demoman, Heavy, Engineer, Medic, Sniper, and Spy), each with their own play style, abilities, weapons, et cetera, et cetera. Each class has his own personality as well. The Scout is cocky and badmouthing, hailing from Massechusets. The Demoman is drunk, Scottish, and obsessed with saying, \"KA-BEUUUUMMM!!!\" The Spy is sneaky, suave, polite and French. The Sniper takes inspiration from Australian adventurers and is always there to lighten the mood. And the Heavy is pootis. All of the classes are delightful to listen to and play around with. I personally have had no problems whatsoever with the framerate, connections, or graphics. Speaking of graphics, the art style is what really sets TF2 out there from the rest of the fps games. It maintains a cartoony, fun feel, while also keeping it gory. Sometimes all you need to lighten up your day is see a cartoon character\'s head get blown off while dancing a Russian clogging dance. Yea, that\'s a thing in this game. You can customize beyond compare in TF2, because of the various weapons, taunts, and most importantly, HATS!! All of these things make it the most unique and entertaining first person shooter experience on Steam. In addition to all that, it\'s free. You can buy weapons and cosmetics for real money in either Steam or the in- game Mann Co. store, but to play costs exactly $0.00.
Cons:
One of the biggest downsides is the microtransaction deal. Throughout your playtime, you may be pressured into wanting to buy  things from the store and you may end up spending a lot of money. You also have to pay for extra inventory space. In your inventory, a box could show up containing cosmetics or weapons. However, you have to pay to open them. The game isn\'t fully available to you. In order to play one of the best modes in my opinion, Mann vs. Machine, you have to pay for a ticket. Another potential con is the chat. People have been known to spam, scam, and just straigt up troll anyone on the server on the chat (which you cannot turn off, by the way). Also, if you have a mic, you can talk to your team. This could be good, right? Well, sort of. Every once in awhile, you can use the chat with your friends to communicate and talk strategy. But 95% of the time, the people WILL NOT STOP TALKING. You will, I repeat, you WILL run into six year olds sounding like a squeaky toy. Fortunatley, you can mute individual players, but you can\'t turn off voice chat permanantley. You need to mute every one of the players at the start of each match to avoid hearing them talk. This just really takes away from the whole experience for me.
Final verdict:
9/10. Why? Because of all the pros, like the diversity, gameplay, gamemodes, servers, teams, cosmetics, uniqueness, and cost. The cons can barely make a dent in the pros. The downsides can be fixed with enough resistance and perserverance. I would wholeheartredley reccomend Team Fortress 2 to amybody looking for a great video game to play. And because it's free, you can play for a bit and just let it go, no harm done. Good job, Valve.
Now make us Half Life 3.

Team Fortress 2 is a very fun and exciting first person shooter. There are 9 classes that vary so greatly and there are many different weapons per class. The classes are scout, soldier, pyro, demoman/demoknight, heavy, engineer, medic, sniper, and last but not least spy. Scout is a fast player who can double jump and requiers aa lot of aiming with the pistol and scattergun. Soldier's rocket launcher has a wide spread attack radius, so you can take out multiple people at once, pyro's main weapon is their flame thrower which leave a large radius of space for you to attack with. demoman has a grenade launcher, stickybomb launcher and a bottle. the grenade launcher throws rolling grenades that explode if they hit an entity or they will just as I said before, roll across the ground for a few seconds. The demoknight ( a branch off of demoman), has a sheild and sword. the sheild allows you to charge at people and the sword has a large range perfect against close range classes. The heavy has the most health in the game, but this also means that he is the slowest. The "heavy weapons guy" weilds a minigun that you must rev up before firing. Next is the engineer AKA the "engi". This class can build sentry guns which are basicly just stationary heavy bots, dispensers that dispence health and ammunition to fellow teammates, and most importantly, teleporters. Teleporters as you may have guessed can teleport teammates to wherever the teleporter exit is. this can be very useful for heavys, soldiers, and other slow-pases classes like that. Then there's the sniper. the sniper holds a sniper rifle which can at full charge 1 hit kill any class with a headshot. he also carries an SMG and a kukri for close-combat. Finally we have the sneaky frenchman, (my personal favorite) the spy. This strategy based class carries a disquise kit, which allows you to disquise as your teammates or your enemies, a knife which allows you to 1 kit kill on a stab from anywhere on the enemy's back, a revolver which can be used to pick off enemy medics and sometimes snipers, and a sapper which "sapps" enemy engineer's buildings. Overall TF2 is a great game with different playstyles to fit everyone's needs. I don't see any reason not to at least try it out. Now seriously, TF2 is a great FPS game. In my case, I wasn't part of the gaming world at all and TF2 happened to be an excellent entry gate. Being free to play let me get a good taste of the game before becoming premium (just any purchase in the market will do... I recommend to go for a key). Now, every game is tough at the start, especially if it's multiplayer. I was lucky to find an online community in which I received a lot of help and improved by leaps and bounds. There are several of these communities online, I'm sure one of them will work for you.
Now, after thousands of hours in game and several others titles played, it just became my favorite game ever. You will have 9 different mercenaries to choose from, all with different features. Depending on the situation, you might want to choose the character that your team needs to win. For each character, also, you will be receiving new guns as you play. These will allow you to try different loadouts that, again, you can modify according to your needs. Just be patient and the game will reward you for playing.
TF2 can be played from a low skill level (granted, it won't be easy... but you will learn fast), and one excellent feature is the high skill level ceiling... You can keep improving permanently. This game is highly re-playable.
Finally, the cosmetics (ah, the cosmetics...) One unique feature of TF2 is the abundancy of cosmetics to personalize your character. You will discover that hats are a big thing in this game. And you will want hats, oh yeah you will.
In summary, I absolutely recommend you to give it a try. It's free!  And, if your case is similar than mine, you might be just about to discover your favorite game ever.

Team Fortress 2 to me is a one of a kind game. Yes, it is an online multiplayer shotter games, like many other on the market. But still.
I strongly suggest for anyone, who loves fps, shoother, class and/or team based genre to try it out. It's free to play, so there's no money risked. But, be warned.
This is a fun AND frustrating game. It's not for everyone, thats for danm sure. It's not those AAA every-year-a-new-episode-is-released shooter type. And it has "flaws" and "weaknesses", as well strenghts and charm. It works differently. The damage system, how the aim works, the roles you fulfill in the team, the classes and how your equipment is changing the style you should play are all takes time, will and practice to get used to.
Don't expect, to be a No.1 360 noscoper topscorer legend on your first run. You will get denied, obliterated. Because all the weapons and characters have their own attributes. And there are player with vastly more experience, who knows all the little trick you will take tens of hours and thousands of death to catch up with. Teamwork is one of the strongest tool at your disposal, keeping on eye on the team composition and avoid overflow of one class (for example all the rageswitch to sniper/spy to get the revenge kill) could mean the difference between win and loss.
I recommned this game for everyone to try out. But if you don't like it move on, instead of depraving it, because you get backstabbed while trying to headshot a Bonked! scout. And don't forget, it is a TEAM and CLASS based game, wich is played for objective primally, not for score and kills.
And this game has one of the most amazing, active and creative community, and they usually come up with amazing contents and even new maps and gamemodes to play on from time to time. If you get bored with one gamemode you will always find another one.
(Oh, of course there are tryhards, whiners trolls and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, but hey, welcome to the internet!)

How To Make a Basic Butter Cake from Scratch
Makes one 2-layer cake
What You Need
Ingredients
1/2 cup unsalted butter, softened (plus extra for greasing the pans)
1 1/2 cups sugar
3 large eggs
2 1/4 cups all-purpose flour
1 teaspoon salt
3 1/2 teaspoons baking powder
1 1/4 cups whole milk
1 teaspoon vanilla
2 1/2 cups buttercream frosting, such as basic buttercream
Equipment
2 9-inch round pans
Stand mixer or hand mixer
Measuring cups and spoons
Cookie scoop or measuring cup, for dividing the batter
Instructions
Heat the oven to 350°F.
Sift together the flour, baking powder, and salt. Set aside.
Prepare the pans: Rub the bottoms and sides of the cake pans with a little butter, shortening, or baking spray. Make sure to get into the corners and all the way up the sides. Flour the sides and bottoms of the pan by scooping a bit of flour into the pan, then shaking and tapping to coat the bottom and sides of the pan with flour; dump out the excess. Alternatively, cut out a parchment round and use this to line the bottom.
Beat the butter and sugar until fluffy and light. Cream together for about 3 to 5 minutes on medium spread (see above notes for more information).
Add the eggs one at a time. Beat until the batter is very smooth and creamy-looking. Adding the eggs one at a time gives them a better chance at incorporating into a smooth batter. Be sure they are room temperature so the batter does not appear curdled.
Beat in half the flour, salt, and baking powder. Add the sifted dry ingredients with the mixer running at low speed. Continue to mix until incorporated.
Beat in the milk and vanilla. Alternate adding in the liquids with the dry ingredients so the milk has a chance to be absorbed without needing to overmix the batter. Stream in the milk with the mixer on low until combined.
Beat in the remaining flour mixture until just combined and no more visible flour remains. Stir a few times with a spatula to make sure no more flour remains on the bottom of the bowl.
Divide the batter between cake pans. Use a scale or mechanical ice cream scoop to evenly divide the batter. Smooth the tops with an offset spatula. Drop the pans against the counter to shake out air bubbles.
Bake for 25 to 30 minutes: When done, the cake should be puffed like a pillow, golden, and pull away from the sides of the pan. When done, a toothpick inserted into the center of the cakes should come out clean.
Cool for 15 minutes in the pan. Run an offset spatula around the cake to make sure it's completely loosened from the sides of the pan.
Flip the rounds out of the pan, remove the parchment lining, and flip right-side up to cool completely.
Once cool, frost and assemble the cake with the buttercream.

I can't think of enough good things to say about TF2. For some people I feel, it's just not for them, but for me, and I know for thousands of other avid TF2 players out there, the confusion and frustration of being a F2P who has no idea what he's doing wore off quickly, and was rapidly replaced by a desire to learn and improve at the game. I didn't want to write this review until I had hit a thousand hours because, really, I wouldn't have felt competant to. In a game where thousands of hours is a norm, there is a lot to learn, and an almost infinite skill ceiling. This game never gets old, and just when you think it has, you find a new minigame, a new community of people who you'll get to know for years to come, a new update with new shiny things to buy, and more. When people talk about the game dying, I scoff because the game they played may be dying. The game that existed over 10 years ago when they first bought the game or first decided to try out because it had just became F2P is gone. But that isn't a bad thing. Because you can be sure that, after you have thousands of hours and have become completely used to all and everything the game can give you, your favorite weapons will change, new game mechanics will be added that forces you to keep learning, keep changing, and most importantly, keep you from getting tired. Your old favorite weapons will be nerfed, and weapons you haven't used in years will come out. People say it's dying because it is a different game, but for every old player who has left because they don't like the change, because they can't deal with suddenly being bad at the game again and losing their well designed perfectly constructed loadouts, there are dozens more gamers who are welcomed to the game for that very reason, and that will play on for just as long as they did, if not longer, because the new generation of gamers welcome that change and look forward to it. To be honest, I still didn't feel equipped to write this review with over a thousand hours on the game, seeing as a quick dive into TF2center will yield full teams and games of people with 3000+ hours, but though the game may change until old players will find it nigh unrecognizable, there is still that underlying spirit, that soul, that simultaneously welcoming and toxic community and that satisfaction with every new skill you master or strategy you discover that is undeniably and undoubtedly TF2, which, for now, I feel I have experienced enough to speak on the matter. For anyone who took the time to read this review, or for the ♥♥♥♥♥ that scrolled down to the bottom, even with all these words there really isn't any way someone could explain the history and jokes and community and the gameplay and the very feeling of TF2 short of writing a book, and after they had, they would have found the game had already had an update bringing new content to the front of our minds, so this was the best way I could sum up the game. I can't recommend it enough, I am completely certain that TF2 will never die. I see enough F2Ps every game I play, and thousands of hours later I believe they will see just as many, if not more, but also just as many old players, getting older, getting more experienced, bringing a new era of meta-games and feedback into the game. If you still haven't started doing it, install it. If you were smart and saw the "Overwhelmingly Positive" rating on the game when you first clicked on the page, you would have already started installing it before you read this review. If you did, it's probably done by now, this review is damn long.

I love this game, there are so many ways to play.  There are nine different classes in TF2 and each plays very differerently it is a bit like owning nine different games (oh, except TF2 is free to play and so I didn't technically have to buy it to 'own' it).
Feel like going bananas and charging straight into the enemy lines?  Go with the Pyro: his (or her?) flamethrower is ideal for the job.  Feel like stalking around and waiting for the opportune chance to strike like Snake?  Go with the Spy.  Heck, you can even get Snake's 'cardboard box' in this game (but you must trade for it, more on this in a moment).  Feel in the mood for some FPS 'tower-defense'-like action (a bit like Sanctum)?   No problem, go with the Engineer.  Build a tower aka Sentry Gun and rain misery and annoyance upon your foes.  Or you can just play Sniper.
You don't need mad, super-fast twitch reaction FPS skills to do well in this game, which is a big reason why I personally like it.  Working cohesively as a team is more important, with each player fulfillling their role all contributes eventually to your team's success.  Also, the scoring system rewards players who play the mission objective.  For example, one mission-type is to push a cart (bomb) along a train track.
Although this is a Free to Play game, I have spent more money on this game than any other.  That's because of something called 'hats'.
So to sum up, download this game because it is lots of fun.

Great game that has intresting game mechnics via a class system. If you are tired of the instant kills, grey paste and random spawning of most first person shooters then this game is the game for you. It is very competitive, has a large skill gap but is easy to play. There is a class for evey play style and a load out for even more customisation on those classes.
The main downsides to this game is the huge skill gap (you will need to put in 1000 hours into it to be consistently good at it although everyone has their magic moments), the saltness of the community and the cheaters using 3rd party programs to see though walls, improve aim and in general give an unearned advantage to them. The saltness is feed by the cheaters because you won't really know if a person who is really good is genuine or not easierly. And the community is very unlikely to kick even a blatant cheater as they tend to win when they have a person using cheats. There will also be very one sided teams quite alot  where one team gets destroyed, especially if you scramble (I think the games matchmaking and scramble algorithms enjoy human suffering). The game sometimes lag like an EA server, but in general it is managable if not perfect.
On the whole you should find this game enjoyable and fun to play especially as it is free. Except for the hats, which you should buy because hats (also buy them from the community market as you can get them alot cheaper then from the shop).

Team Fortress 2.
Where do I begin?
I'm assuming you're considering getting it, so let me sum up why you should in three, long-winded points.
1 - TF2 is a free-to-play game that really means it.
Team Fortress has been free to play for almost half a decade, and it's managed to steer clear of microtransactions and other bull-honkey. The following items that you can pay for in-game are as follows:
- New weapons.
Now, while this may seem the opposite of what I have just said, hear me out. Weapons in TF2 are (compared to other games with unlockable weapons) very, VERY well balanced. Weapons are based around upsides and downsides geared for a certain playstyle or gameplay situation, and no weapons are ultimately more useful than the weapons you automatically get at the start of the game, otherwise known as "stock weapons."
Not to mention, you will frequently find weapons on your own on a random basis, with the game just giving them to you.
- Hats.
As awesome as they are, they have no change on gameplay and are purely cosmetic.
You can also find these with the same random drop system, but they're way rarer.
- Competitive Mode Access and other benefits.
Competitive mode is really not something you need, if I'm being honest. TF2 is a casual game with a decent competitive scene, but nowhere near the scale of Counter-Strike or DOTA. TF2 is a casual game and you are missing nothing playing it causally.
2 - Team Fortress has been around for a LONG time, and will continue to be around for even longer.
The game, (as much as some redditors may complain otherwise) has a team and company behind it that has legitimately helped the game evolve and grow with the times to continue to be new, fresh, and charming. There's something for everyone and everything for someone. TF2 will always continue to impress me and many others in years to come.
3 - The game is some excellent fun.
Team Fortress offers some of the most varied gameplay any video game can offer you. With nine classes with unique roles, weapons, and playstyles, (not to mention all the alternative playstyles other weapons can grant you,) its basic player interaction is already amazing. That's not even to mention the tons upon tons of gamemodes, each offering a brand new, balanced, and overall brilliant spin on the game allowing you to play in more creative and hilarious ways. But remember, it's called TEAM Fortress for a reason. While there may be dpzens of ways to play, there's really only one way to win: work and communicate with your team.
If you're a casual gamer looking for a fun time, a competitive gamer looking for some solid gameplay, or a dedicated gamer looking for true, pixelated love in vidya game form, Team Fortress 2 is for you.

Gameplay - ++++-
Comunity - +++--

Team Fortress 2 (commonly abbreviated as TF2)  is a First Person Shooter game unlike any other.
There is no "Storyline", plot, or cumbersome AI support characters.
There is only you, your guts, your weapon, your team, and the opposing team.
A wide selection of maps  tests you ability to adapt to new surroundings, blind spots, and pitfalls.
Different and unique gamemodes challenge you to use various strategies to achieve that victory everyone vies for.
Nine classes, each with their perks and weaknesses, encourage you to find your perfect fit- and then to improve upon it.
No matter what happens in war, anything and anyone can change the tide.
In this game, everyone has a chance, but not everyone has the patience.
This game is
for those that cannot handle losing or dying in-game. Like any other game, it takes hours, months, years to master, and even those with thousands of hours may insist that they still do not know everything about TF2.
This game is
for those who are lazy or purposely idiotic. Cheaters, Abusers, Microphone Spammers, and Hackers are strongly despised, and Valve inputs effort to ensure a safe yet fun playing experience.
The Steam Workshop for TF2 keeps content fresh, exciting, and inspirational. Vote on your favorite weapons and maps, and Valve
officially add them to the game.
Even if they do not, some items can be still enjoyed without official use.
Some private server owners, for example, may host maps that are not officiated by Valve.
A plethora of weapons and cosmetics allow creative freedom.
Each weapon has its drawbacks and benefits, much like the classes themselves.
Choose which weapons will complement your strategies best.
Cosmetics give your player-character a special look and feel. Whether you want to intimidate the enemy, humor your allies, or just look cool, TF2 has cosmetics to help.
Why wait?
Team Fortress 2 is free, forever.
Give it a go, and grab your

Wow! I'm surprised I haven't done a review of this game already.
I sure loved playing this game, I have a lot of nostalgic memories attatched to this one. What can I say? Back in 2008-2011, I played the absolute life out of this game. Back when you actually had to buy it haha... I actually haven't played it in years so I can't say as to what the game is like now but I will tell you what it was like back when I enjoyed it.
Team Fortress 2 is/was a game about teamwork. You had three game modes which were gold-rush, control point, and CTF
In gold-rush, you had to stand next to a cart and get it to the end of the map for your team to win, the more players that were next to it the faster it would move. At the very end if the team won, the cart (which contained a big bomb) would cause a big explosion causing the other team to then lose.
Control point, well... You stand on a control point for a certain amount of time and capture it before an opponent would try to kill you etc. Once captured, the other team would have to defend themselves at the next one.
There are nine characters you can play as, each one of them has their strengths and weaknesses but if the team your on has the right balance of all of them, then you can win.
Overtime, the game received big updates to each character, e.g Scout, Spy, Sniper, etc. The character would receive new weapons, achievements, and a 'Meet The' video (for some of them). There was also a Soldier vs Demoman event where if there were more kills earned as that particular character, that character would have an extra item which they could use, whereas the other one didn't (I think?)
As the game was filled with more hats and items, the game in my opinion became more unbalanced, right around the time it went free to play when more items were being pushed in; as well as a 'Mann Co.' in-game market where you can purchase weapons and hats.
As soon as the game went free to play, players who had bought the game prior to it being free received one single hat... Which didn't even look all that great. They also had a bigger backpack for weapons and item drops etc. All a player would have to do is purchase £9 or £20 worth of items and they could then have all features availiable to them as if they owned the full game etc.
After it went free, Team Fortress 2 became hat-fortress 2 as the game felt more about wearing some goofy hat and items which no one cares about rather than playing the actual game. Pretty much every game that I played (after it went free) I lost, over and over and over again. But prior to this, I had won 80% of the time.
So do I recommend this game? Yes. But I'm not really recommending the game that it is now, I'm recommending the game I remember more than anything as I haven't played it in years. Maybe one day I'll go back to it, but I doubt it.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding cheese cake recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1 cup digestive plain sweet biscuit crumbs
3 tablespoons sugar
3 tablespoons melted butter
40 ounces softened cream cheese
1 cup sugar
3 tablespoons flour
1 tablespoon vanilla
1 cup sour cream
4 eggs
Directions:
For The base:.
If you're using a dark pan, preheat the oven to 350. If you are using a shiny pan, 375.
Combine the crumbs, melted butter and 3 tbsp sugar well and pat onto the bottom of a 9 inch springform pan. I also like to very very lightly butter the sides of the pan so that the cheesecake will not stick later on.
Bake for 10 mins in your preheated oven and remove. Let it cool while you prepare your batter.
For the batter:.
Make sure everything is at room temperature.
Combine sugar, cheese, flour and vanilla in a big bowl and mix on medium speed till well combined. Don't forget to scrape the bowl as you're doing this.
Mix in the sour cream till its incorporated well. Then, add the eggs one by one, mixing well after each addition.
Pour the batter into the springform and let it bake for 1 hour and 10 minutes After the baking time, turn off the oven and leave the door ajar. Let the cake cool in there for about 1 1/2 hours.
Remove the cake and let it cool thoroughly. Refrigerate overnight.
Release the sides of the springform.
Eat.

Wow! I'm surprised I haven't done a review of this game already.
I sure loved playing this game, I have a lot of nostalgic memories attatched to this one. What can I say? Back in 2008-2011, I played the absolute life out of this game. Back when you actually had to buy it haha... I actually haven't played it in years so I can't say as to what the game is like now but I will tell you what it was like back when I enjoyed it.
Team Fortress 2 is/was a game about teamwork. You had three game modes which were gold-rush, control point, and CTF
In gold-rush, you had to stand next to a cart and get it to the end of the map for your team to win, the more players that were next to it the faster it would move. At the very end if the team won, the cart (which contained a big bomb) would cause a big explosion causing the other team to then lose.
Control point, well... You stand on a control point for a certain amount of time and capture it before an opponent would try to kill you etc. Once captured, the other team would have to defend themselves at the next one.
There are nine characters you can play as, each one of them has their strengths and weaknesses but if the team your on has the right balance of all of them, then you can win.
Overtime, the game received big updates to each character, e.g Scout, Spy, Sniper, etc. The character would receive new weapons, achievements, and a 'Meet The' video (for some of them). There was also a Soldier vs Demoman event where if there were more kills earned as that particular character, that character would have an extra item which they could use, whereas the other one didn't (I think?)
As the game was filled with more hats and items, the game in my opinion became more unbalanced, right around the time it went free to play when more items were being pushed in; as well as a 'Mann Co.' in-game market where you can purchase weapons and hats.
As soon as the game went free to play, players who had bought the game prior to it being free received one single hat... Which didn't even look all that great. They also had a bigger backpack for weapons and item drops etc. All a player would have to do is purchase £9 or £20 worth of items and they could then have all features availiable to them as if they owned the full game etc.
After it went free, Team Fortress 2 became hat-fortress 2 as the game felt more about wearing some goofy hat and items which no one cares about rather than playing the actual game. Pretty much every game that I played (after it went free) I lost, over and over and over again. But prior to this, I had won 80% of the time.
So do I recommend this game? Yes. But I'm not really recommending the game that it is now, I'm recommending the game I remember more than anything as I haven't played it in years. Maybe one day I'll go back to it, but I doubt it.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding cheese cake recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1 cup digestive plain sweet biscuit crumbs
3 tablespoons sugar
3 tablespoons melted butter
40 ounces softened cream cheese
1 cup sugar
3 tablespoons flour
1 tablespoon vanilla
1 cup sour cream
4 eggs
Directions:
For The base:.
If you're using a dark pan, preheat the oven to 350. If you are using a shiny pan, 375.
Combine the crumbs, melted butter and 3 tbsp sugar well and pat onto the bottom of a 9 inch springform pan. I also like to very very lightly butter the sides of the pan so that the cheesecake will not stick later on.
Bake for 10 mins in your preheated oven and remove. Let it cool while you prepare your batter.
For the batter:.
Make sure everything is at room temperature.
Combine sugar, cheese, flour and vanilla in a big bowl and mix on medium speed till well combined. Don't forget to scrape the bowl as you're doing this.
Mix in the sour cream till its incorporated well. Then, add the eggs one by one, mixing well after each addition.
Pour the batter into the springform and let it bake for 1 hour and 10 minutes After the baking time, turn off the oven and leave the door ajar. Let the cake cool in there for about 1 1/2 hours.
Remove the cake and let it cool thoroughly. Refrigerate overnight.
Release the sides of the springform.
Eat.

Introduction:
Team Fortress 2 (TF2) is a free to play team-based first-person shooter multiplayer video game developed and published in October of 2007 by Valve Corporation. It’s the sequel to the 1996 mod Team Fortress for Quake and its 1999 remake. The game contains 9 classes (which offer different playstyles), 11 different game modes, a wide variety of maps (not including custom ones), an insane amount of weapons that can spice up your gaming experience, and “a god knows how many” amount of cosmetics commonly known as hats (that’s why some people call this game the “Hat Simulator”).
Graphics (8.5/10)
The game uses the Source Engine. I must say that this game has great graphics even if it came out in 2007. Although that’s true, it doesn’t look that great when the graphics settings are low since it’s an old engine.
Audio (10/10):
Nothing to comment about it, haven’t found any issues with it.
Gameplay (9/10):
The game delivers an astonishing gaming experience with its diversity. You easily get attached to the game classes and its maps. Same goes with its game modes, really entertaining and unique. When it comes to weapons, I’m a bit disappointed. While the game has a big amount of weapons, some of them are unbalanced, overused or underused, but for the most part the weapons are gameplay changing factor without a doubt. In other words, the same loadout for a class won’t work forever. The loadouts are situational.
Personal enjoyment (9/10):
I’ve being playing this game for quite some time and I must say I’ve really enjoyed it. The biggest problem that I encountered was when I started playing the game. It doesn’t matter if you’re a good at playing Call of Duty or Battlefield or at any other first-person shooter game since most of the skills and knowledge that you acquire in those games cannot be transferred into TF2. In other words, if you know how to play the game, you’re going to be super satisfied and enjoy playing the game but if you don’t, you’re just going to think it’s the worst game ever and immediately uninstall it. Basically, it’s not an easy game to master. It requires a lot patience and practice but once you get the hang of it, oh boy you’re gonna love it.
Overall this game receives a 9.13/10. At least give it a try. This is currently my favourite game of all time.

I have played this game a bit over the years, and I love the game. For people deciding whether to try it out or not, here are some pros and cons.
Pros:
-Diversity among characters: if you don't like one class, try the next.
-Many weapons for each class
-The sense of accomplishment you get when you work as a team
-Free to Play (you have nothing to lose by trying it out)
-Alot of achievements
-Unique gameplay
-Balanced classes, weapons, and maps
-Animation style
-Pretty much bug-free
-Lightheartedness
-Plays great
Neutral
-Can be considered "pay to win", but you can also progress without spending money
-Depth of strategy
-Hats
-You heavily rely on team mates, which can make or break the match
-No bot support
Cons:
-Respawn timers are too long
-Few maps
In all, TF2 is a great game, especially for a F2P. Give it a try!

First of all, I'd just like to say that even though my review is negative, I'll still continue to play this game. You'll read why below.
As you can see, I've played this game for a lot. I think it's a very entertaining game and it can definitely keep you busy for hours. It's fun to earn achievements and be the MVP of a 6-player game. It's satisfying to win a game through hardwork and fair play. Unfortunately, those are the only good things about this game.
There are a couple things about this game that really♥♥♥♥♥♥me off. The biggest problem I have with this game is the community. The community is god awful. Sixty percent of the games you play in tf2, you might not experience proof of a negative community. But, once you play the other 40% and deal with spawn campers, aimbot users, spammers, people who votekick you for no reason, and players who generally think that their hat makes them better than everyone else, you'll realize that what I say is true.
The other negative part of this game is the very overpriced products. I understand that this game needs to stay funded, but it can stay funded AND lower their prices on everything without suffering financially. I mean, half the f**king cosmetics and weapons in this game can range from $2.00 to f**king $100.00. It's legitimately so disappointing that it's so hard to get cosmetic items and rare weapons without spending hundreds of dollars. Still don't think that it's ridiculous? Think of it this way. You can buy yourself an amazing gaming computer for the same amount of money that you can use to buy AT LEAST 6 amazing cosmetic and weapon items in tf2. If you're spending hundreds of dollars on this game, please reconsider your financial choices.
Anyway, that's all I really feel like writing about in my review. I hope this had some effect on your decision to get this game.

Team Fortress 2 is a really fun game. Over the years, it's kept itself fresh with its humour and fun gameplay, with an array of game modes, including Payload, Capture Points, and the co-op mode Mann VS Machine.
Unlike some FPS games, the alternate weapons gained over time do not give you unfair advantages, rather they are situational instead. This means that new players do not necessarily have a massive disadvantage like in other games where players get stronger with the time they put into the game with various upgrades and such. Some of the weapons are purely there for stupidity, such as Scout's Holy Mackerel (FISH KILL!).
On a similar note, the game is not pay to win, because as I already said, the weapons you can buy drop for free and can be traded for as well. You can have the full TF2 experience without paying a penny. All of the perks of going premium in the game are simply for fun, with access to trading, cosmetic drops taunts and other kooky fun stuff the game can throw at you, as well as more inventory space for more stuff. Again though, none of this is needed to get the full experience of the game, which is how a F2P game should be.
Overall, it's a good laugh which will entertain time and time again.

Alright- 230 Hours? Eh, i've come to love it either way.
I'll proceed to describe my experiences on this game.
Alright- Starting out in this game was an interesting experience, starting out on my sisters steam account years ago.
Back then, i hardly knew how to play the game, but from then, after a long gap of time, i started playing yet again, because i enjoyed it the first time around.
Beginning again was a difficult thing, being that my computer is, in the most basic explanation, a literal potato connected to a monitor, but, despite that, i still played. I found that joining small-player servers was the best choice for this Premium potato, and it was then that i joined a server, which i will not name, but has recently gone down (I cry every night), and it was on here that i met some of the best friends i've ever had.
In only 10 minutes of play time i formed great relationships with people i still play with on a regular basis.
This was my first glance at a good community of friends, who were usuals on this server, and i joined them. In the following time my friendships transformed into great relationships full of jokes and fun.
The community of Team fortress 2 does vary, but, is mostly void of rude/dislikeable people as far as i've seen, though, they do exist, and most are there for, as simply as can be put, fun times. I joined a rocketjumping server once, from pure desire to fly like a Hoovy Pidgeon, and i met someone who helped me learn and advance, who is now one of my friends. Thanks to him, i can now fly around maps, and do advanced level stuff.
It's not just in-game that this community exists, however, and aside from the Massive trading community featuring several websites for that purpose, there are people who post videos and tutorials. You can learn, and enjoy alot. From one of these videos, i learned how to play spy better, and since then i have improved quite a bit.
I still remember the first time i actually did a trick stab on someone in a legitimate game (Not when playing with friends on Harvest). The joy i felt still follows me, since, well, it was a few hours ago, but that's besides the point. It's from this community filled with people that i learned to play better and i began to enjoy the game even more.
It is those reasons, i love this game, and i spent money on it, and i continue to play, and plan to play for the visible future.
This is a massive game with a massive community, that is still ever-growing, and if you really want to, you can make incredible relationships with people you have never met in real life, yet, play with regularly, and you can enjoy improving your skill and enjoy the game even more. I find it hard to believe some people don't like this game, but i find it even harder to believe someone hasn't played it once, and even more so, you read this whole mess of text.
You MUST try this game atleast once in your life, because it may make you love it to death, or dislike it for whatever insane reason, especially considering it's a completely free to play game.
Though it may seem hard to get in to, there are people who will help you understand the game better and further enjoy it.
If you've still read thus far, i thank you, and i bid you farewell.

Team Fortress 2 is a really fun game. Over the years, it's kept itself fresh with its humour and fun gameplay, with an array of game modes, including Payload, Capture Points, and the co-op mode Mann VS Machine.
Unlike some FPS games, the alternate weapons gained over time do not give you unfair advantages, rather they are situational instead. This means that new players do not necessarily have a massive disadvantage like in other games where players get stronger with the time they put into the game with various upgrades and such. Some of the weapons are purely there for stupidity, such as Scout's Holy Mackerel (FISH KILL!).
On a similar note, the game is not pay to win, because as I already said, the weapons you can buy drop for free and can be traded for as well. You can have the full TF2 experience without paying a penny. All of the perks of going premium in the game are simply for fun, with access to trading, cosmetic drops taunts and other kooky fun stuff the game can throw at you, as well as more inventory space for more stuff. Again though, none of this is needed to get the full experience of the game, which is how a F2P game should be.
Overall, it's a good laugh which will entertain time and time again.

Am I a Team Fortress 2 Veteran? Hell no.
Do I love this game? You bet.
Listen, hear me out here, this game has many issues, as does every game, but this game is something great. Is this game dead? Well, kinda, but its not Blizzard's fault, it's Valve's for the way they responded to the release of Overwatch. This game is one of the greatest experiences I've had in my adolescent life, and I wish I had played this sooner, because now the community is vanishing. I have hope in this game, I have spend some time and money on this game, have researched some lore, have invested time in TF2 YouTubers. This game isn't dead yet, Overwatch may be winning, and TF2 might not ever come back to life completely, but it holds its spot as the Grandfather of  this genre.
Now, about the actual game itself, when it became free, everyone flocked to it, this game was amazing, and it generated a lot of money for Valve, and they put effort into the game, it was the golden age for TF2. And following the release of Overwatch, Valve made major changes to this game, such as adding a barebones competitive mode that lacked substance and\/or direction, removed vanilla servers, removed ability for mods to be visible in Valve servers, weapon balances, reworks, and more to damage this game's identity. The player count has severely dropped from a few years ago.
This game was something special, and I love it for what it is, a wacky team-based shooting game with interesting classes that specialize in different tasks and are from different places, a place where cosmetics can change social status. This game was a rare gem indeed, and one day I hope it'll be recognized for something great, I plan to show my future kids this game.

How To Make a Basic Butter Cake from Scratch
Makes one 2-layer cake
What You Need
Ingredients
1/2 cup unsalted butter, softened (plus extra for greasing the pans)
1 1/2 cups sugar
3 large eggs.
2 1/4 cups all-purpose flour
1 teaspoon salt
3 1/2 teaspoons baking powder
1 1/4 cups whole milk
1 teaspoon vanilla
2 1/2 cups buttercream frosting, such as basic buttercream
Equipment
2 9-inch round pans
Stand mixer or hand mixer
Measuring cups and spoons
Cookie scoop or measuring cup, for dividing the batter
Instructions
Heat the oven to 350°F.
Sift together the flour, baking powder, and salt. Set aside.
Prepare the pans: Rub the bottoms and sides of the cake pans with a little butter, shortening, or baking spray. Make sure to get into the corners and all the way up the sides. Flour the sides and bottoms of the pan by scooping a bit of flour into the pan, then shaking and tapping to coat the bottom and sides of the pan with flour; dump out the excess. Alternatively, cut out a parchment round and use this to line the bottom.
Beat the butter and sugar until fluffy and light. Cream together for about 3 to 5 minutes on medium spread (see above notes for more information).
Add the eggs one at a time. Beat until the batter is very smooth and creamy-looking. Adding the eggs one at a time gives them a better chance at incorporating into a smooth batter. Be sure they are room temperature so the batter does not appear curdled.
Beat in half the flour, salt, and baking powder. Add the sifted dry ingredients with the mixer running at low speed. Continue to mix until incorporated.
Beat in the milk and vanilla. Alternate adding in the liquids with the dry ingredients so the milk has a chance to be absorbed without needing to overmix the batter. Stream in the milk with the mixer on low until combined.
Beat in the remaining flour mixture until just combined and no more visible flour remains. Stir a few times with a spatula to make sure no more flour remains on the bottom of the bowl.
Divide the batter between cake pans. Use a scale or mechanical ice cream scoop to evenly divide the batter. Smooth the tops with an offset spatula. Drop the pans against the counter to shake out air bubbles.
Bake for 25 to 30 minutes: When done, the cake should be puffed like a pillow, golden, and pull away from the sides of the pan. When done, a toothpick inserted into the center of the cakes should come out clean.
Cool for 15 minutes in the pan. Run an offset spatula around the cake to make sure it's completely loosened from the sides of the pan.
